vignette: A 32-year-old woman's pretransfusion sample shows forward typing: anti-A 4+, anti-B 0; reverse typing: A1 cells 0, B cells 4+.
stem: Which ABO group is most likely?
explanation: Forward typing shows A antigen on red cells (anti-A 4+); reverse typing shows anti-B in plasma (B cells 4+). Concordant results indicate group A.

rationales.A: Correct: A antigen present, anti-B present in plasma = group A.
rationales.B: Group B would react with anti-B in forward typing and show anti-A in reverse.
rationales.C: Group AB reacts with both anti-A and anti-B and has no antibodies in reverse.
rationales.D: Group O reacts with neither anti-A nor anti-B but has both antibodies in reverse.

misconception: Students often memorize the cell reactions but forget that BOTH forward and reverse must agree — reverse typing confirms the plasma antibodies.
examTraps: Forward and reverse must be concordant before the blood group is reported.

vignette: A newborn's forward typing shows group A cells; reverse typing with A1 and B reagent cells shows no reactions.
stem: What is the best explanation for the absent reverse reactions?

choices.text: ABO antibodies are not reliably present in newborns
The baby has the Bombay phenotype

explanation: Newborns do not reliably produce ABO isohemagglutinins (which develop 3-6 months of age); any antibodies present are maternal IgG. Reverse typing is therefore weak or absent in infants.

rationales.A: Secretor status affects soluble substances in body fluids, not reverse typing reactions.
rationales.B: Correct: ABO antibodies develop after birth; reverse typing is unreliable in newborns.
rationales.C: Hemolysis can interfere but does not explain absent reverse reactions specifically in a newborn.
rationales.D: Bombay phenotype (Oh) lacks H antigen and would show anti-H plus anti-A/anti-B — very rare.

misconception: Examinees expect reverse typing to work like in adults; in newborns the forward type is primary.
examTraps: In infants under 4 months, report forward typing and note that reverse grouping is not required.

vignette: A weak D positive patient needs a transfusion of red blood cells.
stem: How should the patient be managed regarding Rh typing?

choices.text: Treat as Rh-positive and give Rh-positive red cells
Treat as Rh-negative and give Rh-negative red cells
Treat as Rh-positive but give Rh-negative plasma
No special consideration; any ABO-identical unit is fine

explanation: Weak D recipients can form anti-D against the missing D epitopes (partial D). To prevent immunization, weak D recipients are treated as Rh-negative and receive Rh-negative red cells. (Weak D DONORS are treated as Rh-positive.)

rationales.A: This is the rule for weak D donors, not recipients.
rationales.B: Correct: recipients who are weak D receive Rh-negative blood to avoid anti-D immunization.
rationales.C: Rh is a red cell antigen; plasma selection does not address D immunization.
rationales.D: Ignoring weak D in a recipient risks anti-D formation and future hemolytic reactions/HDFN.

misconception: The 'weak D donor = positive, weak D recipient = negative' distinction is the classic trap.
examTraps: Remember donor vs recipient handling of weak D.
